analysis.one_liner: Creates a federal job-guarantee program funded by a new tax on stock and bond trades.
analysis.headline: The bill died in committee without a vote or even a single cosponsor, so no jobs program was created and no trading tax was enacted.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill would create a National Full Employment Trust Fund that pays for public-service jobs — housing construction, child care, parks, schools, environmental work — for anyone who has been unemployed and is seeking work. Jobs would pay wages comparable to similar public-sector work in the area. The money would come from a new tax of 0.2% on stock trades and 0.06% on bond and derivative trades, with the Federal Reserve authorized to lend extra if unemployment rises. The bill was referred to two House committees, later to a subcommittee, and never received a hearing, a markup, or a floor vote before the Congress ended.
analysis.who_benefits: Unemployed and involuntarily part-time workers, especially in high-poverty areas, who would be eligible for a federally funded job at public-sector-comparable pay with health benefits, training, and help finding permanent private work. Communities would gain the goods the jobs produce: affordable housing, child care, park and school repairs, and other public services. Local governments and nonprofits would receive grants to run these projects.

how_it_helps.text: The bill sets up Employment Opportunity Grants to fund jobs in areas like affordable housing, child care, health care support, education, parks, and environmental cleanup, with at least 75% of grant money required to go to wages, benefits, and support services like child care [S2].

Eligibility is certified through local one-stop centers for people who are unemployed and seeking work, and workers who refuse a suitable private-sector job offer without good cause lose program eligibility for 30 days — the program is designed as a bridge to regular employment, not a substitute for it [S2].

Wages must be comparable to what public-sector employees earn for similar work in the community, construction work must pay prevailing wages, and at least 35% of workers hired must come from disadvantaged groups unless the local supply is insufficient [S2].
Grants are prioritized for projects serving areas with the highest unemployment, poverty, concentrated poverty, and foreclosures [S2].

analysis.who_pays: Buyers and sellers of stocks, bonds, and derivatives would pay a new federal transaction tax — 0.2% on stock trades and 0.06% on debt and most derivative trades — collected from the exchanges and brokers who process them. Mutual fund trades and initial stock issuances are exempt. The financial industry also bears compliance and reporting costs, and if unemployment rises more than one point, the Federal Reserve must lend the fund additional money, repaid over 10 years.

drawbacks.text: The bill does not contain cost estimates; funding a program that must offer a job to everyone who wants one, paid at public-sector-comparable wages, would require sustained large appropriations, and the securities tax is the sole revenue source [S2].

A trading tax of 0.2% would be passed on to investors, including ordinary people with retirement accounts, and could push some trading volume to foreign markets — a cost an honest supporter would have to acknowledge [S2].

The Federal Reserve would be required to lend the trust fund whatever is needed to keep unemployment within one percentage point of its prior low, and to consider cancelling the debt — a design that gives the central bank an open-ended fiscal role that critics across the political spectrum would contest [S2].

The program's strict anti-displacement and union-consent rules, while protecting existing workers, add administrative complexity and could slow project start-up, which the bill itself anticipates by creating a startup period [S2].

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: For workers who are unemployed long-term, a guaranteed job at local public-sector wages with benefits is a substantial benefit, and the bill's design — requiring job search, refusing displacements of existing workers, and steering workers to private jobs — addresses the most common objections to job-guarantee programs. The unresolved question is scale: the bill provides no funding estimate, and the entire program rests on a single new tax on securities trading plus contingent Federal Reserve lending. Whether the tax would reliably raise enough revenue in a recession, exactly when the program's costs would spike, is unaddressed in the text.

outcome.mechanism: The bill was referred to two House committees when it was introduced, later sent to a subcommittee, and never got a hearing, a committee vote, or a floor vote before the Congress ended.

narrative.text: Rep. Frederica Wilson introduced the Jobs for All Act on April 5, 2024; it was referred to the Committee on Education and the Workforce and the Committee on Ways and Means [S4].
On December 17, 2024, it was referred to the Subcommittee on Work and Welfare; no further action was taken, and the 118th Congress ended on January 3, 2025 with no vote ever scheduled [S4].

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Because the bill never advanced, securities traders and financial firms avoided the new transaction tax, and the public gained nothing from the bill — no jobs were created and no anti-poverty services were funded under it.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: Financial firms avoided the trading tax

for.name: Rep. Frederica Wilson
for.what_they_did: Introduced the Jobs for All Act establishing a National Full Employment Trust Fund funded by a securities transaction tax; the bill drew no cosponsors.

against.name: House Committee on Education and the Workforce
against.what_they_did: Received the bill on referral on April 5, 2024 and later routed it to its Subcommittee on Work and Welfare; no hearing, markup, or committee vote was ever held.

against.name: House Committee on Ways and Means
against.what_they_did: Received the bill on referral on April 5, 2024, which included a new securities transaction tax within its jurisdiction; no action was ever taken on it.

sides.party_line_note: The bill was sponsored by one Democrat with zero cosponsors from either party, so no vote ever revealed whether support would have split by party.

industries.note: The bill imposes a 0.2% tax on stock transactions and 0.06% on debt and most derivatives, paid by exchanges and brokers, plus new reporting duties. Because the bill died, the industry pays nothing; its interest in the bill ran against the program's beneficiaries since its tax would fund them.

industries.industry: Nonprofits and local governments in social services and construction
industries.note: They would have received Employment Opportunity Grants to run job-creation projects in housing, child care, education, and public works. The bill never advanced, so no funding flowed.

The bill bars program jobs from replacing laid-off workers or infringing promotions, and requires union consent before program workers can be placed where a collective bargaining agreement covers similar work — protections for existing workers that also constrain grant recipients.
